Crypto milestones.Bitcoin white paper: Satoshi Nakamoto, whose identity is still unknown, posted it to a cryptography mailing list on Halloween 2008.
Crypto milestones.Bitcoin genesis block: The first block contains a hidden headline from The Times: 'Chancellor on brink of second bailout for banks'.
Crypto milestones.10,000 BTC pizza purchase: Programmer Laszlo Hanyecz paid 10,000 BTC for two pizzas, and 22 May is now celebrated as Bitcoin Pizza Day.
Crypto milestones.Silk Road shut down: The FBI took down the dark-web market and arrested Ross Ulbricht, who got a life sentence and was pardoned in 2025.
Crypto milestones.Mt. Gox collapses: It began as a trading site for Magic: The Gathering cards, once handled most Bitcoin trades, then lost hundreds of thousands of coins.
Crypto milestones.Ethereum launches: Created by Vitalik Buterin, it added smart contracts, programs that run on the blockchain itself.
Crypto milestones.CryptoKitties craze: Collectible digital cats became so popular that they clogged the Ethereum network.
Crypto milestones.El Salvador adopts Bitcoin: It became the first country to make Bitcoin legal tender, though it later scaled the policy back.
Crypto milestones.FTX collapses: Founded by Sam Bankman-Fried, who was later convicted of fraud, it collapsed into bankruptcy within days in November.
Crypto milestones.US spot Bitcoin ETFs approved: The SEC's approval in January 2024 let ordinary investors buy Bitcoin through stock brokers, and the funds drew huge inflows.

Molecules by number of atoms.Hydrogen gas: The lightest and simplest molecule, two atoms of the most abundant element in the universe.
Molecules by number of atoms.Water: Its three atoms are bent at about 104.5 degrees, and water expands as it freezes, so ice floats.
Molecules by number of atoms.Ammonia: Industrial production of it through Haber-Bosch makes fertilizer that helps feed roughly half the world.
Molecules by number of atoms.Methane: The main ingredient in natural gas also comes from cattle, swamps and rice paddies.
Molecules by number of atoms.Ethanol: It has the same formula as dimethyl ether but a completely different structure and behavior.
Molecules by number of atoms.Propane: It becomes liquid under modest pressure, which is why it fits in camping canisters.
Molecules by number of atoms.Benzene: Its ring structure was reportedly inspired by Kekulé's dream of a snake biting its tail.
Molecules by number of atoms.Aspirin: Its ancestor comes from willow bark, and Bayer launched the modern version in 1899.
Molecules by number of atoms.Glucose: The body's main fuel; the brain alone burns about a fifth of the body's energy.
Molecules by number of atoms.Sucrose: Table sugar is glucose bonded to fructose, and it is the biggest molecule on this list.

When these motorcycles debuted.Daimler Reitwagen: Gottlieb Daimler and Wilhelm Maybach built this wooden-framed bike with a petrol engine, regarded as the first motorcycle.
When these motorcycles debuted.First Harley-Davidson: The first was built in a small Milwaukee shed by William Harley and Arthur Davidson.
When these motorcycles debuted.Indian Scout: Indian was America's great Harley rival; the company closed in 1953.
When these motorcycles debuted.BMW R32: BMW's first motorcycle used a flat-twin boxer engine, a layout BMW still builds.
When these motorcycles debuted.Vespa: The name means 'wasp' in Italian; Piaggio built it to get postwar Italy moving.
When these motorcycles debuted.Honda Super Cub: The best-selling motor vehicle in history, with over 100 million built.
When these motorcycles debuted.Triumph Bonneville: Named for the Utah salt flats where Triumph set speed records.
When these motorcycles debuted.Honda CB750: It popularised the superbike, as the first mass-produced four-cylinder bike with front disc brakes.
When these motorcycles debuted.Ducati Monster: Designer Miguel Galluzzi's naked bike rescued Ducati's finances in the 1990s.
When these motorcycles debuted.Harley-Davidson LiveWire: Harley's first electric motorcycle delivers instant torque and near-silent power.

Count the sides (or faces, or panels).Yield sign: Its downward-pointing triangle is unique among road signs, chosen so drivers recognise it from far away and even from behind.
Count the sides (or faces, or panels).Baseball diamond: It is a square, tilted so it looks like a diamond, with the bases 90 feet apart, a distance that has hardly changed since the 1800s.
Count the sides (or faces, or panels).The Pentagon: The headquarters of the US Department of Defense is the world's largest office building by floor area, with five concentric rings.
Count the sides (or faces, or panels).Honeycomb cell: Bees use hexagons because they enclose the most space for the least wax and tile perfectly without gaps.
Count the sides (or faces, or panels).UK 50p coin: Its curved sides form a Reuleaux heptagon, a shape of constant width, so it works in vending machines like a round coin.
Count the sides (or faces, or panels).Stop sign: The octagon shape was chosen so the sign is recognisable even from the back or when covered in snow, unlike other road signs.
Count the sides (or faces, or panels).Canada's loonie coin: Named after the loon bird on its tail side, it was introduced in 1987 and gave the Canadian dollar coin its nickname.
Count the sides (or faces, or panels).Australian 50-cent coin: It is a 12-sided coin, large and heavy for its value, and the sides make it easy to identify by touch.
Count the sides (or faces, or panels).D&D's d20 die (faces): It is an icosahedron with 20 triangular faces, famous as the die used in role-playing games, where a 20 is a critical hit.
Count the sides (or faces, or panels).Classic soccer ball (panels): It is a truncated icosahedron, with 12 pentagons and 20 hexagons, the same shape as the carbon molecule buckminsterfullerene.

Internet firsts.First ARPANET message: UCLA sent the message to Stanford; it was meant to be 'LOGIN', but the system crashed after the first two letters, 'LO'.
Internet firsts.First network email: Ray Tomlinson chose the @ sign to separate the user name from the computer's name, and it stuck.
Internet firsts.First spam email: Gary Thuerk of a computer company mass-mailed hundreds of ARPANET users about a product demo, and it caused an uproar.
Internet firsts.First :-) smiley proposed: Scott Fahlman suggested the sideways smile on a Carnegie Mellon message board to mark jokes.
Internet firsts.First .com domain registered: The domain symbolics.com was the first, registered by a computer company, years before the web took off.
Internet firsts.First website: Tim Berners-Lee built it at CERN to explain the World Wide Web itself, and it still lives at info.cern.ch.
Internet firsts.First text message (SMS): The message 'Merry Christmas', sent by engineer Neil Papworth to a phone in the UK, launched a texting habit that billions share.
Internet firsts.First banner ad: It appeared on HotWired in 1994 for AT&T, asking visitors 'Have you ever clicked your mouse right here? You will.'
Internet firsts.Internet Archive founded: Brewster Kahle's nonprofit archive runs the Wayback Machine, which has saved hundreds of billions of web pages.
Internet firsts.Docomo's original emoji: Shigetaka Kurita designed 176 tiny pictures, 12 by 12 pixels each, and the originals are now held by New York's MoMA.

US rivers by length.Charles: Flowing past Boston and Cambridge, it hosts the Head of the Charles each October, one of the world's biggest rowing regattas.
US rivers by length.Hudson: Its tides reach far inland, nearly to Troy, and the Hudson River School painters made its valley the cradle of American landscape art.
US rivers by length.Potomac: It runs past Washington, DC, whose cherry trees around the Tidal Basin were a 1912 gift from Japan.
US rivers by length.Tennessee: The Tennessee Valley Authority dammed it in the 1930s, bringing power and flood control to one of America's poorest regions.
US rivers by length.Ohio: The Ohio once divided free states from slave states, so crossing it became a powerful symbol for people escaping slavery.
US rivers by length.Snake: It carved Hells Canyon on the Idaho-Oregon border, North America's deepest river gorge at roughly 2,400 metres, deeper than the Grand Canyon.
US rivers by length.Columbia: The largest US river to reach the Pacific, it powers Grand Coulee Dam, one of the biggest concrete structures ever built.
US rivers by length.Arkansas: Despite the state's pronunciation, in Kansas locals say ar-KAN-zas for this river, which starts high in the Colorado Rockies.
US rivers by length.Rio Grande: It forms much of the Texas-Mexico border, where it is called the Rio Bravo, and heavy irrigation can leave it dry before the sea.
US rivers by length.Mississippi: Its name comes from Ojibwe words meaning great river, and New Orleans sits on a delta built from the sediment it carries.

Deep holes and deeper ones.Great Blue Hole (Belize): The Great Blue Hole off Belize is a giant marine sinkhole, popularized by Jacques Cousteau.
Deep holes and deeper ones.Dean's Blue Hole: Dean's Blue Hole in the Bahamas is among the world's deepest sea sinkholes, and it is a famous site for freediving.
Deep holes and deeper ones.Woodingdean Well (hand-dug): The Woodingdean Well in England was dug by hand over many years and is the deepest hand-dug well in the world.
Deep holes and deeper ones.Bingham Canyon Mine: Bingham Canyon Mine in Utah is one of the largest human-made excavations, and it is visible from space.
Deep holes and deeper ones.Lake Baikal: Lake Baikal is the deepest lake on Earth at over 1,600 meters, and it is home to freshwater seals.
Deep holes and deeper ones.Grand Canyon: The Grand Canyon, carved by the Colorado River, is about 1.8 km deep at its deepest point.
Deep holes and deeper ones.Veryovkina Cave: Veryovkina Cave in Georgia is the deepest known cave in the world, explored by cavers over many years.
Deep holes and deeper ones.Mponeng gold mine: Mponeng gold mine in South Africa is one of the deepest mines, where rock temperatures are very high and need cooling.
Deep holes and deeper ones.Mariana Trench: The Mariana Trench holds the deepest point in the ocean, the Challenger Deep, which is deeper than Everest is tall.
Deep holes and deeper ones.Kola Superdeep Borehole: The Kola Superdeep Borehole in Russia is the deepest hole ever drilled, and the project stopped because of the high temperatures.

Australian and New Zealand cities, north.Darwin: Darwin, on Australia's far north coast, is closer to Indonesia than to most Australian cities, and has a tropical climate.
Australian and New Zealand cities, north.Cairns: Cairns is the gateway to the Great Barrier Reef, and it sits in a tropical rainforest region.
Australian and New Zealand cities, north.Brisbane: Brisbane is the capital of Queensland, and has a subtropical climate, and the city is built along a winding river.
Australian and New Zealand cities, north.Perth: Perth is one of the most isolated major cities in the world, and it is closer to Singapore than to Sydney.
Australian and New Zealand cities, north.Sydney: Sydney is Australia's biggest city, and its Opera House has a roof made of over a million tiles.
Australian and New Zealand cities, north.Auckland: Auckland is built on a volcanic field of about 50 volcanoes, and it is New Zealand's largest city.
Australian and New Zealand cities, north.Melbourne: Melbourne is known for its coffee culture and laneways, and it was Australia's capital until 1927.
Australian and New Zealand cities, north.Wellington: Wellington is the world's southernmost national capital, and it's known for being windy.
Australian and New Zealand cities, north.Hobart: Hobart, in Tasmania, is Australia's second-oldest capital city, and it has a lively waterfront.
Australian and New Zealand cities, north.Invercargill: Invercargill is the southernmost city in New Zealand, near the Southland coast, and is the gateway to Stewart Island.

When these sports legends were born.Babe Ruth: Started out as a left-handed pitcher, hit 714 home runs, and the 'Curse of the Bambino' blamed Boston's long drought on selling him.
When these sports legends were born.Jesse Owens: At the 1936 Berlin Games he won four gold medals, a triumph that undercut the Nazi hosts' claims of racial superiority.
When these sports legends were born.Jackie Robinson: Broke Major League Baseball's colour line in 1947, and his number 42 is retired across all teams.
When these sports legends were born.Pele: The only player to win three World Cups, in 1958, 1962 and 1970, he began with the tiny Brazilian club Santos.
When these sports legends were born.Muhammad Ali: Born Cassius Clay, he won Olympic gold in 1960 and changed his name after joining the Nation of Islam in 1964.
When these sports legends were born.Nadia Comaneci: At 14 she earned the first perfect 10 in Olympic gymnastics in 1976, and the scoreboard showed 1.00 as it could not display 10.00.
When these sports legends were born.Michael Jordan: He won six NBA titles and was Finals MVP in all six, but was famously cut from his high school varsity team as a sophomore.
When these sports legends were born.Tiger Woods: He won the 1997 Masters by 12 strokes at 21, and went on to win 15 major golf championships.
When these sports legends were born.Serena Williams: She won 23 Grand Slam singles titles, the most in the Open era, including the 2017 Australian Open while pregnant.
When these sports legends were born.Usain Bolt: His 9.58 for 100 metres and 19.19 for 200 metres, both set in Berlin in 2009, are still world records.

Sediment grain sizes, from mud to monoli.Clay: Its plate-like mineral grains stay stuck together when wet, which is what makes clay moldable for pottery.
Sediment grain sizes, from mud to monoli.Silt: Silt left by the Nile's annual floods fertilized Egyptian farmland for thousands of years.
Sediment grain sizes, from mud to monoli.Very fine sand: This is the finest sand, whose grains you can barely see and which feels almost smooth between the fingers.
Sediment grain sizes, from mud to monoli.Fine sand: Wind lifts and bounces fine to medium grains along the ground, which is how desert dunes form and creep.
Sediment grain sizes, from mud to monoli.Medium sand: Most beach sand sits in this range, though its makeup varies, from white quartz to black volcanic grains.
Sediment grain sizes, from mud to monoli.Coarse sand: Coarse sand drains well, which is why builders prefer it to fine sand when mixing concrete.
Sediment grain sizes, from mud to monoli.Granule: The name comes from Latin for 'little grain', and it marks the step between sand and gravel.
Sediment grain sizes, from mud to monoli.Pebble: Smooth, rounded pebbles are a sign of long travel, tumbled by a river or surf.
Sediment grain sizes, from mud to monoli.Cobble: Cobblestone streets are named for them; these stones range from fist-sized to about head-sized.
Sediment grain sizes, from mud to monoli.Boulder: Boulders carried far from their source by glaciers are called erratics, sometimes stranded on entirely different rock.

First launches of famous rockets.Goddard's liquid-fuel rocket: Robert Goddard launched the first one in Massachusetts; it flew about 2.5 seconds and climbed over 40 feet.
First launches of famous rockets.V-2: In 1944 it became the first human-made object to reach the edge of space.
First launches of famous rockets.R-7 (Sputnik's rocket): It launched Sputnik, and its descendants still carry the Soyuz spacecraft today.
First launches of famous rockets.Saturn V: At 363 feet tall, it remains the most powerful rocket to carry people to the Moon.
First launches of famous rockets.Ariane 1: Europe's first major launcher flew from Kourou in French Guiana.
First launches of famous rockets.Space Shuttle: Columbia flew on its first flight, and it became the first reusable orbital spacecraft.
First launches of famous rockets.Falcon 9: In 2015 its first stage landed upright, a first for an orbital-class rocket.
First launches of famous rockets.Falcon Heavy: On its debut it launched Elon Musk's Tesla Roadster into space.
First launches of famous rockets.NASA SLS: NASA's giant rocket launched the uncrewed Artemis I toward the Moon.
First launches of famous rockets.SpaceX Starship: The most powerful rocket ever built, its first test flight in April 2023 ended in an explosion minutes after liftoff.

How heavy these ancient objects are.A Roman silver denarius: The workhorse coin of Rome, used for centuries; a legionary earned roughly 225 of them a year under Augustus, though its silver content shrank over time.
How heavy these ancient objects are.Tutankhamun's gold mask: The solid gold mask sat directly over the young king's mummy; its braided beard was knocked off in 2014 and clumsily glued back before a proper repair.
How heavy these ancient objects are.Tutankhamun's gold coffin: The innermost of three nested coffins is solid gold, and the priests poured so much anointing oil over it that the resin blackened the surface.
How heavy these ancient objects are.Rosetta Stone: The same decree appears in hieroglyphs, Demotic and Greek, which let Champollion crack Egyptian writing in 1822. It has been in the British Museum since 1802.
How heavy these ancient objects are.Average Great Pyramid block: The pyramid holds an estimated 2.3 million blocks, mostly limestone; far heavier granite beams roof the King's Chamber, and they came from Aswan, about 800 km away.
How heavy these ancient objects are.Average Easter Island moai: Nearly 1,000 moai stand on Rapa Nui, and most were carved from volcanic tuff at one quarry, Rano Raraku. Islanders say they were walked upright.
How heavy these ancient objects are.Average Stonehenge sarsen: The big sarsens of Stonehenge are hard sandstone hauled roughly 25 km, while the smaller bluestones were brought from Wales, about 240 km away.
How heavy these ancient objects are.One of the Colossi of Memnon: Two giant statues of Amenhotep III in Thebes; after an earthquake in 27 BC one began humming at dawn, drawing Roman tourists until repairs silenced it.
How heavy these ancient objects are.Stone of the Pregnant Woman: A Roman-era limestone block abandoned in a quarry at Baalbek, Lebanon, beside even larger ones; it is among the biggest stones ever cut by humans.
How heavy these ancient objects are.The whole Great Pyramid: Built around 2560 BC for Pharaoh Khufu, it was the tallest human-made structure on Earth for about 3,800 years, until Lincoln Cathedral's spire topped it.

The ten Sikh Gurus, in order.Nanak: Founder of Sikhism, born in 1469 in what is now Pakistan, he taught belief in one God, equality, and honest work.
The ten Sikh Gurus, in order.Angad: He is credited with standardizing the Gurmukhi script used to write Punjabi, and with gathering Nanak's hymns.
The ten Sikh Gurus, in order.Amar Das: He made the free community kitchen, the langar, mandatory, and it is said that even Emperor Akbar sat on the floor to eat there.
The ten Sikh Gurus, in order.Ram Das: He founded the city of Amritsar and dug the pool around which the Golden Temple was later built.
The ten Sikh Gurus, in order.Arjan: He compiled the first Sikh scripture, built Harmandir Sahib, and was martyred under Mughal Emperor Jahangir.
The ten Sikh Gurus, in order.Hargobind: He wore two swords, symbolizing spiritual and worldly authority, and built the Akal Takht across from the Golden Temple.
The ten Sikh Gurus, in order.Har Rai: Known for gentleness, he kept a herbal medicine garden and a menagerie, and treated Dara Shikoh, the Mughal prince.
The ten Sikh Gurus, in order.Har Krishan: He became Guru at about five and died of smallpox at about eight, after caring for the sick in Delhi.
The ten Sikh Gurus, in order.Tegh Bahadur: He was executed in Delhi in 1675 after refusing to convert, and is honored for defending religious freedom, including for Hindus.
The ten Sikh Gurus, in order.Gobind Singh: He founded the Khalsa in 1699 and named the Guru Granth Sahib the eternal Guru, ending the line of human gurus.

World cities from west to east.Honolulu: Its name is usually translated as 'sheltered bay', and Pearl Harbor, just to the west, was the target of the 1941 attack.
World cities from west to east.Mexico City: Built on the drained bed of Lake Texcoco over Aztec Tenochtitlan, it has parts that still sink by centimeters every year.
World cities from west to east.Rio de Janeiro: Christ the Redeemer, finished in 1931, looks over the city from Corcovado peak, which rises over 700 meters above the bay.
World cities from west to east.Reykjavík: The world's northernmost capital of a sovereign state, it is heated largely by geothermal hot water from the ground.
World cities from west to east.London: The Greenwich prime meridian, the zero line of longitude, passes through the city's east, so London sits almost exactly at 0 here.
World cities from west to east.Cairo: The Great Pyramids of Giza stand on its western edge, and its metropolitan area holds well over 20 million people.
World cities from west to east.Mumbai: Built on seven islands joined together by reclamation, it is the home of Bollywood, India's huge Hindi-language film industry.
World cities from west to east.Singapore: This city-state became independent in 1965 and packs roughly 5.5 million people onto an island under 750 square kilometers.
World cities from west to east.Tokyo: The greater Tokyo area is the most populous metropolitan area in the world, with well over 35 million residents.
World cities from west to east.Sydney: Jørn Utzon's Opera House opened in 1973, and its roof shells are covered in roughly a million glossy tiles.

When these odd sports began.Underwater hockey: Also known as Octopush, players with snorkels and short sticks push a puck along the pool bottom.
When these odd sports began.Pea shooting championship: These championships are held in Witcham, Cambridgeshire, where pea shooters fire at a target.
When these odd sports began.Lawn mower racing: It started in a British pub as a cheap alternative to motor racing.
When these odd sports began.Worm charming championship: Contestants in Cheshire coax earthworms up from a patch of ground using vibrations, no digging allowed.
When these odd sports began.Elephant polo: Each elephant has a driver, and players swing very long mallets, with Nepal hosting the best-known tournament.
When these odd sports began.Bog snorkelling: Swimmers in flippers and snorkels race along a water-filled trench cut in a Welsh peat bog.
When these odd sports began.Wife carrying: A Finnish sport, with the winner traditionally getting the wife's weight in beer.
When these odd sports began.Air guitar championship: Held in Oulu, Finland, contestants are judged partly on 'airness', which is how convincingly they fake it.
When these odd sports began.Extreme ironing: It was founded in Leicester by Phil Shaw, and players iron in unusual places such as mountains.
When these odd sports began.Chess boxing: Rounds of chess alternate with rounds of boxing, and the game ends by checkmate or knockout.

Darts by the numbers.Darts per turn: A turn is three darts, which is why a score of 180 is the maximum, and why the crowd roars for it.
Darts by the numbers.Darts in a perfect leg: Called a nine-darter, a perfect leg finishes 501 in just nine darts, and it's the rarest and most celebrated feat in the sport.
Darts by the numbers.Numbers around the board: The board's numbers are not in order but arranged to punish wild throws, placing high numbers next to low ones.
Darts by the numbers.Outer bull: The outer green ring of the bull, which counts 25, sits around the red bullseye in the center.
Darts by the numbers.Bullseye: The bullseye, the small red center, is worth 50, and it can be used to finish a leg as a double.
Darts by the numbers.Treble 20: Triple 20 is the standard place to aim, and hitting it scores 60, the highest of any single dart.
Darts by the numbers.Bull height from floor (in): A dartboard's bullseye is hung 5 feet 8 inches off the floor, and the throw line, the oche, is 7 feet 9.25 inches away.
Darts by the numbers.Highest checkout: The biggest finish with three darts is 170: two trebles of 20, then the bullseye. The checkout needs a double to end.
Darts by the numbers.Max score with three darts: Three triple 20s add up to 180, and a perfect score of that kind is called a maximum or a 'one hundred and eighty'.
Darts by the numbers.Starting score: Pro games count down from 501 and must finish on a double, so a lucky high score is never quite enough.

Zoo weigh-in day.Meerkat: Meerkats stand on their hind legs on sentry duty while others forage, warning the group of danger.
Zoo weigh-in day.Flamingo: Flamingos get their pink color from carotenoid pigments in their food, such as shrimp and algae.
Zoo weigh-in day.Koala: Koalas sleep up to 20 hours a day because eucalyptus leaves give so little energy, and have fingerprints like humans.
Zoo weigh-in day.Emperor penguin: Emperor penguins huddle together through Antarctic winter, and males incubate the egg on their feet for about two months.
Zoo weigh-in day.Chimpanzee: Chimpanzees share about 98 percent of their DNA with us, and they make and use tools, such as stick probes for termites.
Zoo weigh-in day.Giant panda: Pandas eat bamboo for up to 14 hours a day, though they have a carnivore's digestive tract.
Zoo weigh-in day.Gorilla: Gorillas eat mostly leaves, shoots and fruit, yet a silverback male can weigh around 160 kg, a lot of salad.
Zoo weigh-in day.Polar bear: Polar bears have black skin under their translucent fur, and they can swim for days.
Zoo weigh-in day.Giraffe: A giraffe's neck has the same seven neck bones as ours, though each can be over 25 centimeters long.
Zoo weigh-in day.Asian elephant: Asian elephants are smaller than African elephants, and have smaller ears, and can eat up to 150 kg of food a day.

Children's classics, by publication year.Alice in Wonderland: Lewis Carroll, whose real name was Charles Dodgson, first told it to Alice Liddell on a boat trip.
Children's classics, by publication year.Treasure Island: Robert Louis Stevenson's pirate yarn popularised many pirate staples, like treasure maps and a one-legged sailor.
Children's classics, by publication year.The Wonderful Wizard of Oz: In the book Dorothy's slippers were silver; they became ruby for the 1939 film to show off Technicolor.
Children's classics, by publication year.The Tale of Peter Rabbit: Beatrix Potter first told it in a letter to a sick child, Noel Moore, in 1893.
Children's classics, by publication year.The Wind in the Willows: Kenneth Grahame first told these tales as bedtime stories to his young son.
Children's classics, by publication year.Winnie-the-Pooh: The bear was named for a real Canadian black bear called Winnipeg at the London Zoo.
Children's classics, by publication year.Charlotte's Web: E. B. White's tale of a spider saving a pig was inspired by a spider he watched on his farm.
Children's classics, by publication year.The Cat in the Hat: Dr. Seuss wrote it using only 236 different words, after a challenge to write a primer kids wouldn't find boring.
Children's classics, by publication year.Where the Wild Things Are: Maurice Sendak originally planned wild horses, but swapped them for monsters because he couldn't draw horses.
Children's classics, by publication year.The Very Hungry Caterpillar: Eric Carle designed it with die-cut holes, inspired by a hole punch, and it has been translated into dozens of languages.

When these American bridges opened.Eads Bridge, St. Louis: It was the first major American bridge to use steel in its trusses, and engineers sank caissons deep below the Mississippi to build it.
When these American bridges opened.Brooklyn Bridge: After its chief engineer died of tetanus, his son took over; P. T. Barnum marched 21 elephants across in 1884 to prove it was safe.
When these American bridges opened.Williamsburg Bridge: When opened, it was the longest suspension span in the world at about 1,600 feet.
When these American bridges opened.Manhattan Bridge: The name of neighbourhood DUMBO stands for 'Down Under the Manhattan Bridge Overpass'.
When these American bridges opened.Hell Gate Bridge: This steel arch over the East River later became the model for Australia's Sydney Harbour Bridge.
When these American bridges opened.George Washington Bridge: It is often called the world's busiest motor vehicle bridge, and it first opened with only a single deck.
It is really two bridges joined at Yerba Buena Island, and its east span was replaced in 2013.
When these American bridges opened.Golden Gate Bridge: Its colour is 'International Orange', chosen to stand out in the fog and complement the surroundings.
When these American bridges opened.Mackinac Bridge: Locals call it 'Mighty Mac'; it joins Michigan's two peninsulas and is about five miles long.
When these American bridges opened.Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge: The towers are slightly farther apart at the top than at the base, to account for the Earth's curvature.

Strange units of mass.Dalton: The dalton is the unit of atomic mass, named for chemist John Dalton. It is defined as one twelfth of a carbon-12 atom.
Strange units of mass.Grain: Originally the weight of a single grain of barley, it's still used for bullets and arrow shafts. A pound has 7,000 of them.
Strange units of mass.Carat: Carats measure gemstones, and the name comes from carob seeds used as balance weights. A five-carat diamond weighs only a gram.
Strange units of mass.Scruple: An old apothecaries' unit, equal to 20 grains. It gave us the word for a small doubt, from the Latin for a tiny sharp stone.
Strange units of mass.Ounce: Its "oz" abbreviation comes from the Italian onza. A fluid ounce of water weighs roughly an ounce, which is a handy coincidence.
Strange units of mass.Pound: The abbreviation "lb" comes from the Latin libra, which also gives us the pound sterling's £ symbol. The unit is about 454 grams.
Strange units of mass.Stone: One stone is 14 pounds, and people in Britain and Ireland still give their body weight in stones. It started as the weight of a real stone.
Strange units of mass.Slug: A slug is the imperial unit of mass, with a name that's easy to remember. It's the mass a one-pound force accelerates at one foot per second squared.
Strange units of mass.Hundredweight (US): The US hundredweight is 100 pounds, but the British one is 112 pounds. The "hundred" refers to a count of older units.
Strange units of mass.Short ton: A US short ton is 2,000 pounds, compared with the British long ton of 2,240. The metric tonne is 1,000 kilograms.

How thick these flow (viscosity).Air: Barely any resistance: air is a fluid too, and unlike liquids it gets thicker as it warms.
How thick these flow (viscosity).Acetone: The solvent in nail polish remover flows even more easily than water and evaporates in moments.
How thick these flow (viscosity).Water: Water at about 20 degrees Celsius is the yardstick; the unit 'poise' honours Jean Poiseuille, who studied blood flow.
How thick these flow (viscosity).Milk: Fat and protein make it slightly thicker than water, which helps give milk its creamy feel.
How thick these flow (viscosity).Olive oil: Warming thins it dramatically, which is why oil glides across a hot pan.
How thick these flow (viscosity).Glycerin: Syrupy and mildly sweet, it turns up in soaps and cough syrups and absorbs moisture from the air.
How thick these flow (viscosity).Honey: Honey's thickness depends heavily on water content and temperature; a warm jar pours far more easily than a cold one.
How thick these flow (viscosity).Ketchup: Ketchup is shear-thinning: it sits thick until shaken or tapped, then suddenly runs.
How thick these flow (viscosity).Peanut butter: Spreading it thins it for a moment; natural jars separate, with the oil floating on top.
How thick these flow (viscosity).Pitch (tar): A famous Queensland experiment has watched it drip only about once a decade since 1927, which shows how thick it is.

Radio frequencies used by these technolo.AM radio: It travels farther at night, when the ionosphere bounces signals back, which is how stations reach far across the continent.
Radio frequencies used by these technolo.NFC tap-to-pay: A tap-to-pay phone powers the card's tiny chip through magnetic induction, which works only within a few centimetres.
Radio frequencies used by these technolo.FM radio: Edwin Armstrong invented it in the 1930s to give static-free sound, and it sits around 88 to 108 MHz.
Radio frequencies used by these technolo.GPS (L1 signal): Signals from satellites reach your phone weaker than the background noise, yet receivers can still pick them out.
Radio frequencies used by these technolo.Bluetooth: Named for a Danish Viking king, Harald Bluetooth, and it shares its band with microwave ovens.
Radio frequencies used by these technolo.Wi-Fi's faster band: It carries data faster than the older 2.4 GHz band but struggles to pass through walls.
Radio frequencies used by these technolo.Satellite TV (Ku band): Heavy rain can fade the signal, which is why storms sometimes freeze satellite dish TV.
Radio frequencies used by these technolo.5G millimeter wave: It can be extremely fast but reaches only a few hundred metres and can be blocked by walls and even leaves.
Radio frequencies used by these technolo.WiGig: Oxygen absorbs signals at this frequency, so it works only within a room.
Radio frequencies used by these technolo.Fiber-optic light: At about 193 THz it corresponds to light at 1,550 nm, in the infrared and invisible to the eye.

Diggers and burrowers by weight.Garden ant: A colony may hold thousands of ants working in tunnels, and queens of some species live for 15 years or more.
Diggers and burrowers by weight.Naked mole-rat: Almost cancer-free and able to live for 30 years or more, this hairless rodent lives in colonies ruled by a single queen, like bees do.
Diggers and burrowers by weight.Mole: Moles have broad, spade-like front paws and almost no sight. Their velvety fur lies flat in either direction so they can move backwards in tunnels.
Diggers and burrowers by weight.Puffin: Unlike most seabirds, puffins nest in burrows on clifftops. They can hold a dozen or more small fish crosswise in their colourful beaks.
Diggers and burrowers by weight.Meerkat: Meerkats take turns as sentries, standing on hind legs to watch for danger and calling out warnings. They live in tunnel networks in southern Africa.
Diggers and burrowers by weight.Rabbit: A rabbit warren can have dozens of entrances, and the animals thump their hind legs to warn of danger. Their teeth never stop growing.
Diggers and burrowers by weight.Groundhog: Also called a woodchuck, it hibernates in a deep burrow. On Groundhog Day in the US, its shadow is said to predict six more weeks of winter.
Diggers and burrowers by weight.Badger: Badgers dig huge setts with many chambers, and they change the bedding regularly, bringing in dry grass. Some setts have been used for hundreds of years.
Diggers and burrowers by weight.Wombat: This Australian marsupial produces cube-shaped droppings, which it uses to mark territory. Its backward-facing pouch stops soil from getting in while digging.
Diggers and burrowers by weight.Aardvark: Its name means earth pig in Afrikaans. It digs rapidly for termites at night and can slurp up tens of thousands of insects in a single meal.

Growing tomatoes, step by step.Sow seeds indoors: Tomatoes start early indoors in late winter because they need a long, warm season. They came originally from the Andes of South America.
Growing tomatoes, step by step.Seedlings poke up: The first two leaves to appear are seed leaves, not true tomato leaves. The leaves that follow are the typical feathery, scented ones.
Growing tomatoes, step by step.Move into their own pots: Transplanting, or pricking out, gives each seedling room to grow. Tomatoes can grow roots from their stems, so they can be buried deep.
Growing tomatoes, step by step.Harden off outdoors: Plants are gradually introduced to the outdoors over a week or so, to toughen them against wind and cold. Skipping this step can shock them.
Growing tomatoes, step by step.Plant in the ground: Tomatoes need warm soil and plenty of sun, and should be planted after the last frost. Planting them deep encourages a stronger root system.
Growing tomatoes, step by step.Tie stems to canes: Indeterminate tomatoes grow like vines and need support. Gardeners also pinch out side shoots to focus the plant's energy on fruit.
Growing tomatoes, step by step.Yellow flowers open: Tomato flowers are self-pollinating, but a bit of shaking or buzzing from bees helps. Each yellow flower may turn into a fruit.
Growing tomatoes, step by step.Little green fruits form: Botanically, a tomato is a fruit, specifically a berry. In 1893, the US Supreme Court nonetheless ruled it a vegetable for tariff purposes.
Growing tomatoes, step by step.Fruits ripen red: Ripening is triggered by the gas ethylene. Tomatoes come in many colours as well, from yellow to purple and even striped.
Growing tomatoes, step by step.Pick and eat: Tomatoes taste best if kept out of the fridge, since cold dulls their flavour. A ripe one picked warm from the vine is hard to beat.

Home Alone, in story order.Kevin sent to the attic: Home Alone (1990) was filmed in Winnetka, Illinois, where the real house used for the McCallisters' home is still a tourist stop.
Home Alone, in story order.The family oversleeps: Macaulay Culkin was only ten when the film was shot, and it made him one of the biggest child stars of the early 1990s.
Home Alone, in story order.Mom realizes on the plane: Catherine O'Hara plays Kevin's mother, and her frantic attempt to get back from Paris to Chicago is a comic subplot of its own.
Home Alone, in story order.Kevin's grocery run: The film's pizza and grocery scenes helped make it a holiday staple, and Little Nero's pizza is a spoof of mobster movies.
Home Alone, in story order.Church chat with Marley: Old Man Marley is played by Roberts Blossom, who was also a published poet, and whose scary reputation turns out unfounded.
Home Alone, in story order.Kevin sets the booby traps: The burglars are Harry and Marv, played by Joe Pesci and Daniel Stern, who earned the nickname the Wet Bandits for their calling card.
Home Alone, in story order.Paint cans down the stairs: The swinging paint can that clobbers Harry is one of the film's best-remembered gags, and it was real slapstick built with props.
Home Alone, in story order.Marley rescues Kevin: Marley's shovel rescue pays off his reputation, and it also reunites him with the son he had been estranged from.
Home Alone, in story order.Police nab the Wet Bandits: John Williams's score includes Somewhere in My Memory, a song which earned an Oscar nomination for Best Original Song.
Home Alone, in story order.Mom comes home: John Hughes wrote the film, which grossed over 470 million dollars worldwide and became one of the biggest comedies ever made.

Nelson Mandela's life, in order.Born: Mandela was born Rolihlahla, a name meaning troublemaker, and a teacher gave him the English name Nelson on his first day at school.
Nelson Mandela's life, in order.Co-founds ANC Youth League: The ANC Youth League was co-founded with Oliver Tambo and Walter Sisulu, and it pushed the ANC toward more active protest.
Nelson Mandela's life, in order.Arrested: Mandela was arrested in August 1962 near Howick while travelling disguised as a chauffeur, and was first jailed for leaving the country illegally.
Nelson Mandela's life, in order.Sentenced to life: At the Rivonia Trial he said an ideal of democracy was one for which he was prepared to die, and he was spared death.
Nelson Mandela's life, in order.Released from prison: He spent 27 years in prison, including 18 on Robben Island, before his release was televised around the world.
Nelson Mandela's life, in order.Nobel Peace Prize: He shared the Nobel Peace Prize with F. W. de Klerk, the president who released him and helped end apartheid.
Nelson Mandela's life, in order.Elected president: He became the first black president of South Africa in the country's first fully democratic elections.
Nelson Mandela's life, in order.Steps down: Mandela chose to serve only one term, which set an example for peaceful transfer of power on the continent.
Nelson Mandela's life, in order.Appears at World Cup final: Mandela appeared at Soccer City for the 2010 World Cup final, a frail but beloved presence, and the stadium roared.
Nelson Mandela's life, in order.Dies: He died on December 5, 2013, aged 95, and since then his birthday, July 18, has been marked as Mandela Day.

Resting heartbeats per minute.Blue whale: The largest animal ever has a heart the size of a small car, and its heartbeat can be detected from some distance.
Resting heartbeats per minute.Elephant: Elephants have strong slow hearts, and the rhythm helps explain why large animals tend to live longer than small ones.
Resting heartbeats per minute.Horse: Racehorses can have a resting rate as low as about 30, and in a gallop that can climb above 200 beats a minute.
Resting heartbeats per minute.Cow: A cow's heart beats about once per second, and their hearts beat faster in warm weather or when under stress.
Resting heartbeats per minute.Human: A typical adult rests at 60 to 100 beats a minute, and trained endurance athletes can drop well below 50.
Resting heartbeats per minute.Dog: Small dogs tend to have faster hearts than big ones, with tiny breeds beating over 120 times a minute.
Resting heartbeats per minute.Cat: A cat's heart beats about twice as fast as ours, which is why a cat's pulse is hard to feel by hand.
Resting heartbeats per minute.Chicken: Birds generally have fast hearts, and a chicken's is quick enough to supply energy for flapping.
Resting heartbeats per minute.Mouse: With a heart rate of around ten beats per second, mice tend to live only a few years.
Resting heartbeats per minute.Hummingbird: When feeding, its heart can beat over 1,200 times a minute, yet at night it enters torpor and slows dramatically to save energy.
